meta.baseline_narrative: I'm Jeroen van Bemmel. I design and build systems that make complex technology practical to adopt and sustainable to operate. My work spans carrier networks, cloud infrastructure, automation, and AI-powered applications. The common thread is simple: make complexity manageable through architecture, models, and automation.

baseline_exit.text: Thank you for watching. meta.global_guidance: I want to understand how Jeroen approaches complex technical problems and what kind of systems architect he is today. Please guide me through the experience most relevant to evaluating him for senior technical architecture, systems engineering, infrastructure, networking, or AI systems roles. I am particularly interested in how he has helped organizations adopt new technologies and move them from experimental or manually operated systems toward structured, repeatable, and sustainable operation. Look for evidence of architectural judgment, hands-on engineering depth, customer and organizational adoption, automation, model-driven systems, and the ability to make complex technology operational in the real world. Do not simply present his career chronologically. Instead, identify the strongest evidence for these capabilities and show me the most relevant path through the presentation. I want to explore the presentation based on what I am trying to understand, rather than simply follow a chronological career history.

entries.text: My foundations are at Bell Labs. From 2001 to 2006 I was a research and development engineer at Lucent Technologies, designing and implementing carrier-grade signaling systems. I was focused on a fundamental engineering problem: what happens when protocol models on paper have to run concurrently in the real world? I built HPJSS, a high-performance Java SIP stack for carrier service platforms, which enabled the Lucent Service Broker product to meet its performance KPIs for commercial launch. I also worked on multiprocessor scheduling, distributed signaling, and protocol-oriented infrastructure. I contributed to European research projects and conference publications, including SIP message prioritization work that appeared in the Bell Labs Technical Journal in March 2006. Across my career I am an inventor on 33 U.S. patents; SIP message prioritization from this Bell Labs work is one of them. That is where my control-plane engineering started.

entries.text: HPjSS++ is direct evidence of my production-grade, high-performance C++ systems programming. I built a complete SIP signaling stack from Linux sockets upward: UDP, TCP, and SCTP transports; a buffer-oriented parser; RFC 3261 transaction state machines; dialogs; authentication; and higher-level signaling services. The maintained source tree is roughly fifty-one thousand seven hundred lines across two hundred thirty-five C and C++ files, including runnable user-agent and stateful proxy applications. Its performance strategy was architectural, not cosmetic: size resources from an expected traffic profile, preallocate transaction and receive state, minimize copying with string views and lazy parsing, and make ownership and lifetime boundaries explicit. Concurrency is handled through atomic state transitions, locks, timer queues, retransmission, cancellation, and timeout machinery. This is the kind of systems work where protocol correctness, memory behavior, concurrency, and network I/O all have to hold together under sustained load.

entries.text: MyOS is the project where I explored systems architecture all the way down to the hardware. Over roughly a decade, from 2002 through 2012, I built an experimental freestanding thirty-two-bit x86 operating system in C++ and assembly. It spans the complete path from boot and memory management through interrupts, multiprocessing, threads, device drivers, filesystems, and a TCP/IP stack with services such as DHCP. The central design idea was to organize kernel facilities as versioned components and interfaces, with XML models and XSLT-generated composition making dependencies and initialization order explicit. MyOS3 evolved that architecture from one statically linked kernel into a small resident Core and an ELF-loadable Atmosphere module containing higher-level drivers, networking, and services. The Core loader relocates the module and resolves its imports against exported kernel symbols, while both partitions continue to communicate through the same interfaces and shared runtime context. This project demonstrates not only low-level implementation depth, but a long-running interest in making complex systems modular, inspectable, and evolvable.

entries.text: From 2019 through 2024 at Nokia, I worked with strategic enterprise and cloud customers to modernize data center networking through SR Linux, EVPN fabrics, and automation — bridging legacy infrastructure with next-generation operational models. One of the biggest barriers to EVPN adoption was the need for a disruptive big-bang migration. I developed the SR Linux EVPN Proxy to bridge static VX-LAN and dynamic EVPN fabrics, enabling customers like Eurofiber to modernize incrementally while maintaining operational continuity. Schema-driven orchestration and validation approaches kept automation correct across distributed network platforms.

entries.text: In October 2022, at the Open Compute Project Future Technologies Symposium in San Jose, I presented Open Compute Heat Appliances for Exergy. The idea was sustainable, decentralized compute: repurpose retired data-center CPUs and GPUs as connected heat appliances. That extends hardware life past the usual refresh cycle, reuses compute heat for buildings, and returns capacity to a distributed cloud. Connectivity lets charging be coordinated to help balance renewable supply on the grid. Scaling that pattern needs open standards — which is why OCP is a natural home for the work.

entries.text: In February 2024, I co-presented Compute Differently with Dan Desjardins at Civo Navigate in Austin. The idea was to rethink sustainable value creation. Instead of assuming that more computing demand must always mean more concentrated infrastructure, we asked what value could be created from capacity that already exists — CPUs and GPUs in phones, enterprises, and telecommunications infrastructure. We explored a model where workloads are measured, computing capacity is contributed across a network, and value is shared with the participants providing the resources. We demonstrated the concept live by creating an ad-hoc compute cloud from devices in the audience, then scaled the same pattern to a larger astrophysics workload across partner compute groups. For me, this brought together distributed systems, network architecture, sustainable computing, and a broader question: how can technology create more value from the resources we already have?

entries.text: That operational thread continues into xFrame from Exergy Infinity LLC — towards model-driven systems. The same model-driven principles used in infrastructure engineering are applied here to AI-assisted content and knowledge workflows. xFrame explores how domain models become the foundation for reliable, reproducible communication systems — transforming structured source into documents, dashboards, presentations, and multimedia through deterministic build pipelines. Author once in a declarative format; compile through an intermediate representation into multiple delivery targets. Provenance and reproducibility stay first-class so outputs can be reviewed, regenerated, and evolved as the model changes. AI-assisted generation is constrained through schemas, templates, and explicit transformation stages rather than prompt-to-output workflows. Open source includes xYang for semantic validation, and xFrame dot AI publishes tools and agent skills — while the presentation compiler remains an Exergy product. This extends the operational model-driven approach from network infrastructure into AI-enabled systems.

jeroen_van_bemmel.headline: Systems Architect — Intent-to-Execution Platforms, Knowledge Systems, and Agentic AI Governance
jeroen_van_bemmel.summary:
Systems architect and software engineer with 25+ years of experience designing distributed systems, orchestration platforms, and high-performance infrastructure software across telecommunications and large-scale compute environments, including work at Nokia and Bell Labs. Specialized in building deterministic execution and validation systems for heterogeneous distributed infrastructure, with deep expertise in protocol semantics, concurrency control, resource scheduling, and control-plane/data-plane separation.

Focused on reducing operational complexity in large-scale systems through state minimization, schema-driven execution models, and predictable runtime behavior under high concurrency. Experienced in designing infrastructure mechanisms that balance correctness, scalability, and fault tolerance across dynamic environments, including distributed orchestration, execution routing, and automated configuration enforcement.

Strong background in translating abstract system constraints into efficient, production-grade architectures with emphasis on scalability, observability, and graceful degradation under failure conditions.

work_experiences.description: Founder building model-driven systems that turn structured source into reliable documents, dashboards, presentations, and AI-assisted workflows—applying the same schema-and-validation approach used in infrastructure engineering to knowledge and communication systems.

Influenced infrastructure automation strategy in a high-complexity, rapidly changing environment by introducing structured models for inventory, lifecycle state, and operational change.
